Hello — this is the launch post for the EDI blog.
[EDI](https://github.com/kapelner/EDI) (Experimental Design and Inference) is
an R package for randomized experimental designs — fixed designs like
blocking and optimal MILP-based allocation, sequential designs like
matching-on-the-fly and covariate-adaptive randomization — paired with
inference procedures matched to each design and response type. We'd like to
start with a post about something we needed in order to trust EDI on real
data, not just simulations: a large collection of real, completed randomized
experiments to replay through it.

EDI ships with a comprehensive test suite built mostly on *synthetic* data:
real covariate structure, simulated treatment assignment, simulated
response — necessary for coverage/power validation, where you need to
know the ground truth to check whether an interval actually covers it.
But synthetic data can't validate one thing: does EDI correctly replay a
**real, already-completed** randomized experiment's actual assignment
mechanism and actual outcome? For that we needed real trials. This post
is about finding 262 of them, what they look like, and running one
through EDI end to end.

## Finding them: five rounds, the last one exhaustive

The search (documented in full in
[`experimental_datasets.md`](https://github.com/kapelner/EDI/blob/main/R/package_metadata/experimental_datasets.md))
went through five rounds of increasing thoroughness:

- **Rounds 1–4** (27 datasets): repository search for known dataverses
  (the Hayes & Moulton *Cluster Randomised Trials* textbook companion,
  8 datasets), CRAN package-metadata keyword search (5 datasets), then a
  **deep CRAN scan** pre-filtered to CRAN's ~9,700 `LazyData`-true
  packages, scored against a domain keyword set, with the top 692
  actually inspected (12 more confirmed).
- **Round 5** (203 more datasets, the big one): after round 4's
  keyword/`LazyData` pre-filtering was flagged as a real limitation — it
  can miss a genuine dataset just because its title doesn't match a
  keyword — round 5 instead checked **every one of CRAN's 25,043 scanned
  packages' actual source tarballs for a real `/data` directory**. No
  title, description, or field filtering at all. **11,173 of 25,043
  (44.6%) had one.** Excluding the 630 packages already covered by
  earlier rounds left 10,543 genuinely new candidates, each mechanically
  harvested — tarball download, extract, `load()`/`fread()` the data
  directly, parse the `.Rd` help page — **without ever running
  `install.packages()`**. That produced ~13,150 dataset-level rows; every
  one flagged by a "random"-language regex (2,607 of them) was reviewed
  in full by five parallel AI review passes against one rigor bar —
  explicit textual confirmation of random assignment to a real completed
  study, excluding synthetic/simulated data, random *sampling* (not
  *assignment*) language, aggregate/meta-analysis tables, and duplicates
  — plus a ~600-row random spot-check of the *non-flagged* rows (zero
  additional confirms there, which is what validates the regex flag as a
  reliable prioritization signal rather than a lucky shortcut). 236
  candidates were confirmed before deduplication; 203 survived as
  genuinely new entries after removing repackaged duplicates (the same
  Freireich 1963 leukemia trial and the same NIMH schizophrenia trial,
  for instance, each turned up under 2–4 different CRAN packages).

## What 262 real experiments look like

The result: **262 datasets, 278 dataset×response-type pairs**, covering
every one of EDI's six response types —

| Response type | Core (pre-sweep) | Total (with round 5) |
|---|---|---|
| continuous | 8 | 129 |
| survival | 9 | 47 |
| incidence | 16 | 43 |
| count | 7 | 26 |
| ordinal | 3 | 17 |
| proportion | 2 | 16 |

— sourced three ways: 20 direct CRAN packages (`survival`, `medicaldata`,
`geepack`, `AER`, …, extracted without installing them — more on that
below), one GitHub-only package with no CRAN listing
(`itamarcaspi/experimentdatar`), and the rest from Harvard Dataverse
mirrors of J-PAL/IPA field-experiment archives and openICPSR studies.

Three usage modes, not mutually exclusive: **covariate-source only** (real
baseline covariates, synthetic response with known truth — same pattern
as EDI's existing synthetic-benchmark datasets); **real assignment
replay** (real covariates *and* real observed treatment assignment,
synthetic response — validates inference against an actual realized
randomization rather than an idealized one); and **full real replay**
(real covariates, real assignment, real outcome, nothing synthetic — a
genuine case study, what the demo below does). One dataset,
`IVdataset` (Angrist & Krueger 1991), was evaluated and explicitly
excluded: it's observational census data analyzed via an instrumental-
variable strategy, not a randomized experiment — there's no real treatment design `W` to
redraw from.

One important constraint: **none of this real data ships with EDI or
lives in this repository.** ICPSR/openICPSR terms prohibit
redistribution without written agreement, and the CRAN-sourced ones stay
exactly where CRAN already hosts them. The whole pipeline fetches live,
cleans, converts to CSV and then 
caches locally in compressed tar.bz2 files.

## The download script

[`download_experimental_datasets.R`](https://github.com/kapelner/EDI/blob/main/R/package_metadata/download_experimental_datasets.R)
handles two genuinely different retrieval mechanisms, one per dataset
depending on where it lives:

**CRAN and GitHub packages, without `install.packages()`.** For a dataset
that's just one object inside an R package's `data/` directory, the
script downloads the package's own **source tarball** directly from
`https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/`, `untar()`s it, and reads the
one `.rda` file it actually needs straight out of `data/` — no
`install.packages()`, no polluting the library, no dependency resolution.
If the pinned version has since been superseded on CRAN's main listing
(likely, since the round-5 sweep alone took hours across many parallel
workers, and packages update continuously), it falls back to CRAN's
`Archive/<pkg>/` for that exact version, and only as a last resort to
whatever's currently on CRAN — deliberately never a silent substitution
that could swap in a changed dataset, just a version-string mismatch that
essentially never changes the classic dataset a package exists to ship.

**Harvard Dataverse, with no account needed.** Confirmed working
end-to-end: fetch the dataset's metadata to find the target file's
numeric id and whether a "Guestbook" is required (a usage-tracking
questionnaire some depositors attach — unrelated to the file's license,
and satisfied with plain identity fields, not credentials); if so, `POST`
a guestbook response to get back a signed download URL; then follow the
resulting HTTP 303 redirect to a short-lived, pre-signed S3 URL. One real
gotcha found the hard way: guestbook "options"-type answers must be
submitted as the option's **string text**, not its numeric id — the
numeric form looks equally plausible and 500s server-side with an opaque
`ClassCastException` instead of a helpful error.

Every dataset, regardless of source, ends up normalized to **plain CSV**
(`.tab` retabbed, `.dta` read via `haven` and stripped of value/variable
labels, zip-bundled files unzipped and the target member located
recursively), and the whole output directory is packed into one
`randomized_experiment_datasets.tar.bz2` — uniform format, and CSV text
compresses well under bzip2 (two of the source zips alone are 99MB and
221MB; only one small member file is kept from each after conversion, the
rest discarded).

## Showing one off: a dermatology RCT

`mice::toenail` is one of round 5's 203 new finds (the `mice` package's
own copy is identical to the classic `toenail`/`toenail2` dataset also
distributed via `DPpackage` and `HSAUR3`) — a multicenter randomized trial
comparing two oral antifungal treatments for toenail onychomycosis
(De Backer et al. 1998, *Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology*).
294 patients, randomized essentially 50/50 (148 to itraconazole, 146 to
terbinafine so the desig is assumed to be a "Bernoulli" design), followed over seven visits with the degree of nail
separation scored at each one.

The raw data is longitudinal — up to 7 rows per patient — so replaying it
through EDI's fixed-design framework needs one response per subject. We
used each patient's outcome at their **last recorded visit**
(0 = none/mild nail separation, 1 = moderate/severe) as the response (incidence type), and
their **baseline (first-visit) severity** plus **number of visits
completed** as covariates — both measured before, or as a byproduct of,
the randomized treatment, not affected by it.

Fetching it hit the same Archive fallback logic as before: the pinned
`mice` version had already been superseded on CRAN's main listing by the
time this ran, so `cran_download_dataset_as_csv()` fell back to
`src/contrib/Archive/mice/`, found the exact pinned version there, and
extracted `toenail.rda` straight out of the tarball — no
`install.packages()`.

This is the **full real replay** mode: real covariates, the trial's
*actual* recorded treatment assignment (not a fresh draw), and the
*actual* recorded outcome — run through `InferenceSuite`, which discovers
every applicable inference procedure for an `incidence`-response fixed
design and reports one Cauchy-combined p-value across all of them. The
Cauchy combination test turns a set of (possibly dependent, possibly
correlated) p-values into one omnibus p-value by transforming each to a
standard Cauchy variate and averaging, which — unlike Fisher's or
Stouffer's methods — has a known closed-form null distribution that holds
under arbitrary, unknown dependence between the inputs, with no need to
estimate a correlation structure.[^cauchy]

```r
library(EDI)

# download_experimental_datasets.R packs each dataset into its own
# <name>.tar.bz2 (here mice_toenail.tar.bz2, containing mice_toenail.csv,
# one row per visit) -- unpack it and collapse to one row per patient:
untar("mice_toenail.tar.bz2", exdir = ".")
raw <- read.csv("mice_toenail.csv")

baseline <- setNames(raw[raw$visit == 1, c("ID", "outcome")], c("ID", "baseline_severity"))
n_visits <- setNames(aggregate(visit ~ ID, raw, max), c("ID", "n_visits"))
final <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(raw, raw$ID), function(d) d[which.max(d$visit), ]))
final <- final[, c("ID", "outcome", "treatment")]
names(final)[names(final) == "outcome"] <- "final_outcome"
tn <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "ID"), list(baseline, n_visits, final))

n <- nrow(tn)
X <- tn[, c("baseline_severity", "n_visits")]
w <- as.integer(tn$treatment)          # 0 = terbinafine, 1 = itraconazole -- the REAL randomized assignment
y <- as.integer(tn$final_outcome)      # 1 = moderate/severe separation at last visit, 0 = none/mild

des <- DesignFixedBernoulli$new(n = n, response_type = "incidence", verbose = FALSE)
des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des$overwrite_all_subject_assignments(w)  # replace the internal draw with the trial's real assignment
des$add_all_subject_responses(y)

suite <- InferenceSuite$new(des)
set.seed(1)
res <- suite$run_all_inference(
  screen = TRUE, plots = FALSE, num_cores = 1L,
  methods = c("wald", "score", "lik_ratio", "rand"),
  max_secs_per_class = 60
)
```

And the real output — 25 model-fits across 13 incidence inference
classes (simple/pooled-variance mean difference, binomial-identity
regression, CMH, exact Zhang, g-computation risk difference/ratio,
log-binomial, logistic regression, Miettinen–Nurminen, modified Poisson,
Newcombe, probit regression, plain risk difference), each fit with
whichever of `wald`/`score`/`lik_ratio` applies to it:

A real, if borderline, treatment effect: itraconazole patients were less
likely to still have moderate/severe nail separation at their last visit
(8/148 = 5.4%) than terbinafine patients (17/146 = 11.6%), and that
direction holds consistently across all four estimable estimand groups —
mean difference, log-odds, log risk ratio, and probit marginal all land
between p = 0.06 and p = 0.07, agreeing with each other in both sign and
rough magnitude. None individually clears the conventional 0.05 threshold
on its own at this sample size, and the Cauchy-combined p-value across all
23 inferences (p = 0.066) reflects that honestly — a real trial with n=294
and a 6-percentage-point difference in a fairly rare outcome sits right at
the edge of what that sample size can resolve, and EDI reports it as such
rather than rounding up to "significant." `Exact Zhang` and one `score`-method
Log Binom fit report a point estimate but no usable p-value in this run —
also shown as-is, not smoothed over.

## Try it yourself

The full manifest, licensing notes, and every dataset's provenance are in
[`experimental_datasets.md`](https://github.com/kapelner/EDI/blob/main/R/package_metadata/experimental_datasets.md);
the download script is
[`download_experimental_datasets.R`](https://github.com/kapelner/EDI/blob/main/R/package_metadata/download_experimental_datasets.R).
The same `DesignFixedBernoulli` + `overwrite_all_subject_assignments()` +
`InferenceSuite` pattern above works identically on any of the other 261
datasets — survival, count, proportion, ordinal, or continuous.

**Links:** [EDI on GitHub](https://github.com/kapelner/EDI) ·
[EDI docs](https://kapelner.github.io/EDI/)

    Structures. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*,
